title: Those who mourn (Matthew 5:4)
hookLine: blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted

lines: THE SECOND LINE OF THE SERMON.
cards: Grief gets a polite schedule. A few days off work. A card.

Then, gently, the world expects a person to be fine. People say stay strong, or at least they're in a better place, and mean it kindly. But sometimes a grieving person needs someone who will let them be sad.
The second line of Jesus's sermon goes somewhere few would expect. After the empty-handed, he congratulates the people who are crying.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted." The Greek word for mourn, pentheo, is used for mourning the dead: grief that shows, not a quiet sigh.
Jesus doesn't say, blessed are those who get over it. Christians have read this in a few ways.

teach.h: FOR THE LOST, AND FOR THE WRONG.
teach.b: Grief for someone you've lost. Grief over the wrong in the world, and over your own wrongs, as some early Christian teachers read it. And the prophet Isaiah had promised one who would come to comfort all that mourn.
Jesus seems to be saying: that's now. The second word worth opening is comforted.

In Greek it's a form of parakaleo, which can mean to call to your side. It's the same family as the word John's Gospel uses for the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, which the King James Bible translates the Comforter.
So this comfort isn't a pat on the back from across the room. It's someone called in to sit beside you. And notice what it doesn't say.
It doesn't say you won't mourn, or that your grief is wrong or weak. Jesus himself wept at the tomb of his friend Lazarus.
Paul later tells Christians not to sorrow as others which have no hope: not to stop sorrowing, but to sorrow with hope.
That's the beatitude: grief that is real, and comfort promised to it.

how: Christians keep funerals and memorial prayers for the dead, and some churches hold services for those grieving, especially around All Souls' Day or in the dark weeks before Christmas.

o: to beg out loud for help in a time of need
to grieve openly, as for someone who has died
to sit in silence and fast after a hard loss

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: the Bible tells Christians not to grieve
Paul says sorrow not as others which have no hope: grieve, with hope.
comforted comes from a word meaning to call to your side
parakaleo, the same family as the Paraclete.
Jesus wept at the tomb of his friend
at the tomb of Lazarus, in John 11.

games.q: a friend is grieving hard, weeks after everyone else has moved on. what does the beatitude point you toward?
o: give them space until they're over it.
games.why: comfort in Greek means called to your side. the beatitude doesn't hurry grief; it promises company in it.

practice: Think of someone you know who has lost something this year: a person, a marriage, a job, their health.
Don't plan a speech; just ask what it would look like to sit beside them: a message that says I'm thinking of you, no reply needed, a meal, a walk. If you pray, you can name them before God.

wordCard.voice: Pentheo, the Greek word for mourn, grief that shows. The second beatitude: the ones who grieve out loud are blessed, because someone will come to their side.

orig.note: Greek: they shall be comforted. from parakaleo, to call alongside; the Paraclete comes from the same root.

carryVoice: Your line: mourning is not the end. Comfort is promised to grief, not to getting over it. See you tomorrow.
